job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: The year 1857 marked a turning point in Indian history, often remembered as the First War of Independence. While the introduction of greased cartridges served as the immediate spark, the discontent had been brewing for decades due to deep-seated grievances. Peasants and zamindars were heavily burdened by high taxes and rigid revenue collection, leading to widespread resentment across rural India. Simultaneously, the British policy known as the Doctrine of Lapse allowed the Company to annex kingdoms only if a ruler died without a natural male heir, which directly affected leaders like Nana Saheb, the adopted son of the last Peshwa. Furthermore, the British government passed the Act of 1858, which transferred power from the East India Company directly to the British Crown, ending the Company's rule. To prevent future uprisings, the British reorganized the army, reducing the proportion of Indian soldiers and increasing the number of European troops. Throughout this period, Christian missionaries operated independently, though their activities often created social friction. The revolt was not merely a military mutiny; it was a massive uprising fueled by economic exploitation, political annexation, and the fear of cultural interference that eventually forced the British government to overhaul its entire administrative structure in India.

items.evidence: While the introduction of greased cartridges served as the immediate spark, the discontent had been brewing for decades due to deep-seated grievances.
items.q: What role did the greased cartridges play in the revolt of 1857?
options: They set off anger built up over years
They were the one and only cause
They came only after the revolt had ended
They caused the peasants' anger over taxes
items.explain: The cartridges were only the immediate spark; discontent had been growing for decades.

wrong.why: thinks the cartridges alone caused the revolt
mixes up the order of events
joins two separate causes as cause and effect

items.evidence: Peasants and zamindars were heavily burdened by high taxes and rigid revenue collection, leading to widespread resentment across rural India.
items.q: Which example shows the revolt was more than a soldiers' uprising?
options: Villagers resented heavy taxes and strict revenue rules
Sepoys disliked the new greased cartridges
Peasants stayed calm while only sepoys complained
Missionaries worked as officers of the government
items.explain: Peasants and zamindars were angry about high taxes, so anger spread across rural India too.

items.evidence: Simultaneously, the British policy known as the Doctrine of Lapse allowed the Company to annex kingdoms only if a ruler died without a natural male heir, which directly affected leaders like Nana Saheb, the adopted son of the last Peshwa.
items.q: Why did the Doctrine of Lapse affect Nana Saheb?
options: He was an adopted son, not a natural heir
He was the Peshwa's own son by birth
He was a ruler the British wished to remove
He was the leader of the sepoys at Meerut
items.explain: The Doctrine applied when there was no natural male heir, and Nana Saheb was only adopted.

wrong.why: thinks Nana Saheb was the Peshwa's biological son
thinks the British could take any kingdom at will
mixes up rebel leaders and the Meerut march

items.evidence: Furthermore, the British government passed the Act of 1858, which transferred power from the East India Company directly to the British Crown, ending the Company's rule.
items.q: What happened to the East India Company after the Act of 1858?
options: It lost its power to rule India
It went on ruling India until 1947
It received extra power from the Crown
It hired missionaries as government workers
items.explain: The Act of 1858 gave power to the British Crown, ending the Company's rule.

wrong.why: reverses the direction of the power transfer

items.evidence: To prevent future uprisings, the British reorganized the army, reducing the proportion of Indian soldiers and increasing the number of European troops.
items.q: After 1857, how did the British try to stop another revolt in the army?
options: By cutting the share of Indian soldiers
By adding many more Indian soldiers
By sending the European troops back home
By banning only the greased cartridges
items.explain: The British reduced the proportion of Indian soldiers and added more European troops.

wrong.why: reverses what happened to European troops
thinks the cartridges were the only problem
